citing_sentences: We present ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework for cross-environment agent data synthesis (Figure 2).

To explicitly model these implicit tool relations, we organize $\mathcal{M}$ into a typed tool-composition graph $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{TS}}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},w)$ that can chain different services into one tool world (Figure 2).
To collect long-horizon chains that preserve real logical connections, we perform State-Aware Random Walks on $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{TS}}$ (Stage 2 of Figure 2).

citing_sentences: To verify that ToolSpace’s gains do not stem from overfitting to benchmark-like environments, we rank environment clusters by relevance to each benchmark using BGE (Chen et al., 2024) embeddings, and compare SFT on (i) the full data, (ii) only the top-50% most relevant environments (Top-50%), and (iii) a random 50% of environments (Random-50%) (Figure 9(a)).

As shown in Figure 9(b), Agent-World synthesizes all 2,724 files in the sample, whereas ToolSpace synthesizes only 1,218 files associated with operation-bearing environments—1,506 fewer files, or a 55.3% reduction.

abstract:
Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

Contact: dongguanting@ruc.edu.cn, dou@ruc.edu.cn

Project Page: https://toolspace-agent.github.io/

Github: https://github.com/dongguanting/ToolSpace

Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/dongguanting/toolspace

sections.body: Current environment scaling synthesizes a database and scenario first, then derives tools and tasks. This can mismatch real tool interfaces, leave tool compositions ungrounded in execution, and rarely span more than one environment. ToolSpace reverses the order. It mines data, state, and retry edges from execution traces using deterministic rules, clusters the weighted graph into environments, and synthesizes databases only for state-mutating environments. State-aware random walks with rollback produce tasks with assertion checks, and only samples that replay successfully from the initial state are kept. On AutomationBench Pro and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking Pro, seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points relative to the standard versions.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Data-centric synthesis derives tools after databases, so tool interfaces may not match real services; ToolSpace starts from execution traces instead.

sections.body: Simulator-style methods use an LLM as a textual world model to emulate tool feedback, which is cheap but prone to hallucination and state inconsistency. Executable-environment methods synthesize databases, tools, and verifiable tasks programmatically, but the unit of scaling remains the environment, so which tools may compose is fixed in advance. Graph-based agent data synthesis walks API or function-signature graphs. ToolSpace instead mines edges by deterministic rules from adjacent real calls across environments. It types each edge as data, state, or retry, weights it by witnessed frequency, and admits a walk to training only after replay from the initial state passes state, trace, and output checks.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior environment scaling fixes tool composition before drawing tasks, whereas ToolSpace composes tools from observed executions.

sections.body: The section defines tool-use tasks as agent policies producing tool-call sequences over an environment with a persistent database and state space, scored by a verifier. It then describes data-centric synthesis, where a database is sampled first, tools are derived conditioned on it, and tasks follow. Cross-environment reachability is undefined there, because tools from different database pairs share no typed relation. The tool-centric problem asks for four outputs: a typed tool graph built from traces, environment clusters aggregated by edge density, on-demand data for operation environments, and a dataset of task, verifier, tool chain, and initial snapshot. Each chain must satisfy dependency reachability, state preconditions, and parameter provenance, and must pass replay verification from the initial state.
sections.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Tool-centric synthesis requires walks on a typed graph whose chains replay from the initial state.

sections.body: ToolSpace collects trajectories from real MCP services and open agent corpora, grouped by execution authenticity. Adjacent calls yield data, state, and retry edges by deterministic rules with no LLM judgment. Each edge is weighted by observed transition frequency, where $N_{ij}$ counts how often $v_{j}$ immediately follows $v_{i}$ and $N_{i}$ counts occurrences of $v_{i}$. Clusters with $K=804$ environments are formed by connection density. Databases are synthesized only for operation environments, while stateless environments reuse cached tool results. State-aware random walks with rollback produce chains, which are decompiled into tasks and kept only if re-execution from $s_{0}$ passes all checks. The paper reports 77,760 nodes and 34,376 synthesized trajectories, and notes that every edge is witnessed by real adjacent calls.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Deterministic rules build the tool graph, and only walks that replay from the initial state become training data.

sections.body: The Pro versions extend AutomationBench and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking by linking tools that share data or state with benchmark tools, then walking with larger chain length and environment count than the originals. Three doctoral-level experts reviewed all candidate tasks and verification scripts over two days, and a task was kept only if at least two approved it. Agreement was Fleiss' kappa of 0.82 with observed agreement of 93.1%. On AutomationBench, average tool calls rise from 26.8–43.6 under Standard to 56.3–60.6 under Pro. On $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking, they rise from 23.1–32.2 to 27.3–36.3.
sections.heading: AutomationBench Pro and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking Pro
sections.headline: Expert-reviewed Pro versions of two benchmarks, with 300 and 98 tasks, require more tool calls than standard splits.

sections.body: Seven long-horizon benchmarks are evaluated against proprietary models, open-weight models above 200B parameters, and 7–8B and 27–35B environment-scaling models. ToolSpace is trained on three backbones: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and GLM-5.2 at 744B, with the 35B model reaching 43.2 with RL. Training uses one epoch of supervised data and GRPO for reinforcement learning. Decontamination removes trajectories that overlap evaluation test sets. In the 35B component ablation, LLM-judged edges score 37.8 on AutomationBench against 45.8 for full ToolSpace, and removing any component lowers all five ablated benchmarks. Local results are averaged over three independent runs, and external scores are used as published.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: ToolSpace lifts Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6 across seven benchmarks.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the method: deterministic mining of data, state, and retry dependencies from execution traces, clustering into environments, on-demand database synthesis, and replay-verified tasks. It repeats the Pro results, with seven frontier models dropping by up to 38.2 points, and the gains on seven benchmarks, including 23.0 to 41.0 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 44.6 to 56.6 for GLM-5.2. It states that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones and that performance keeps improving with data and environment scale. The conclusion does not add new experiments or state limitations beyond those in earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Conclusion restates that replay-verified, execution-witnessed composition drives gains and scales with data and environments.
